study.title: Isaiah 66 The holiness of God, the consolation of Zion and the final judgment
study.overview: Isaiah 66 contains the book with a strong contrast between the outside religion and the humble heart, between the false security of the rebels and the hope of those who tremble before the word of the LORD. The chapter shows God rejecting any human attempt to limit it to a temple or empty rites, welcoming the contrites, comforting Jerusalem and gathering a large people among the nations. At the same time, it ends with a severe warning: God's judgment on the rebels is real, public and terrible. The chapter unites restoration and judgment, glory and shame, consolation and condemnation.

outline.title: God cannot be reduced to temple or empty worship
outline.explanation: The Lord affirms his sovereignty over all creation and makes it clear that he is not restricted by buildings or external sacrifices. He looks at the humble, the downcast of spirit and for what trembles before his word. In contrast, those who insist on their own ways, reject the divine voice and choose what displeases God attracts punishment upon themselves.

outline.title: Comfort with the faithful and the promise of a surprising restoration
outline.explanation: The word passes to whom the LORD fears and is rejected because of God's name. Though they are despised by hostile brethren, they will hear that shame will fall upon the opposers. Then the image of childbirth describes the sudden and extraordinary birth of a people: Zion, before entering pains, already sees children appear surprisingly, because God himself begins and completes this work.

outline.title: Joy in Jerusalem, divine consolation and judgment on impurity
outline.explanation: Jerusalem is presented as a place of comfort, abundance and joy for those who love and wept for it. The LORD promises peace, the glory of the nations and maternal care, showing that his hand will be known among his servants. But the same God will come in fire to judge all flesh, especially those who sanctify themselves by idolatrous practices and become disgusting in their eyes.

outline.title: Meeting of nations, universal worship and the final scene of horror
outline.explanation: God announces that he will gather nations and tongues together to see his glory and send survivors to the distant regions, so that his fame may be proclaimed among the peoples. Gentiles will also be brought as an offering to the LORD, and some will even be separated for priestly service. The promise is of permanence: new heavens and new earth support the continuity of God's people. Finally, all will stand to worship, while the rebels will have before them the terrible scene of their irreversible judgment.

study.context: The chapter itself indicates a community marked by tension: there are people who tremble through the word of the Lord and there are people who hate and cast out the faithful because of the name of God. The notes provided also link the chapter to the contrast between trust in the temple and true divine acceptance, as well as showing their relationship with the expectation of Zion's restoration and the rejection of the rebels. Without leaving the text and the notes, the scenario is that of a people in religious crisis, in which God promises comfort to the humble and judgment to those who persist in rebellion.
study.theology: The theology of the chapter emphasizes that God is transcendent and sovereign over heaven and earth, but also attentive to the humble heart. True worship is not merely ritual: God is pleased with the breaking, submission to his word and sincere obedience. There is a clear theme of separation between the righteous and the wicked: those who reject the word face judgment, while those who fear the LORD receive comfort, joy and inheritance. The chapter also broadens hope: the glory of God reaches the nations, and the people gathered before him includes those brought from afar. Finally, the last scene affirms the seriousness of the divine judgment, which is not symbolic only, but a real warning about the final ruin of the rebels.

scholarViews.insight: The central point of the beginning of the chapter is that the kingdom of God extends over all creation; therefore, it cannot be limited to a temple or to a human building.
The prophet comforts those who tremble before the word of God, distinguishing them from the ungodly so that they may not be confused with the judgments that fall upon the rebel nation.
The fire and worm of the verse point, in the commentator's reading, to the eternal punishment of the ungodly, the language that Jesus applies to the judgment in Gehenna.

questions: Is my religion more marked by external rites or a humble and obedient heart before the word of God?
Have I rejoiced at the comfort that God offers to his servants, or have I resisted his discipline and his call to repentance?
How does the hope that God brings together peoples of many nations leads me to participate in their mission with reverence and sobriety?
study.practice: Read the chapter as a double call: humble yourself before the word of God and reject all merely outward faith; at the same time, console and encourage those who tremble before the Lord. In practice, examine whether there is any area in which you are relying on religious appearance, repent with sincerity and try to obey in a concrete way. He also prays that God will use his life to welcome, strengthen and not crush those who already suffer because of his name.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided are excerpts and do not cover each verse in a detailed manner; therefore, some chapter connections have been summarized based on the biblical text and the available observations. The historical reading was maintained at a general level, without stating dates, places or reconstructions that are not explicitly supported by the notes. It is also possible that evangelical interpreters emphasize in a different way the relationship between Israel, Zion, the nations and the final consummation, although all the main elements of the chapter have been preserved here.
